newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica 97/98 maize plantings fall 7 pct - producers.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica 97/98 maize plantings fall 7 pct - producers.

text.p: South Africa's maize plantings for the 1997/98 season have fallen by almost seven percent from last year, the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said on Friday.

Nampo said it had warned that a large harvest would depress maize prices and the drop was a result of Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom's decision to abolish a market floor price at the end of the current season on April 30.

The producer body said commercial plantings of white maize had dropped by over 12 percent to 1.636 million hectares, but yellow maize had increased by just over one percent to 1.368 million hectares. There was uncertainty about plantings in the non-commercial sector, it said.
Japie Grobler, Nampo's chairman, said the outlook for the maize already planted remained good, with expectations of average to above-average rainfall predicted for the months of February and March.
He said the next three to four weeks were the most critical for the harvest.
"In this regard we are somewhat concerned as an increasing number of maize areas are starting to dry out...if the rains begin too late, crops will definitely be damaged," Grobler said.
However, a bumper harvest carried the risk of depressing prices to such an extent that producers would not be able to afford to plant enough maize later this year to meet domestic demand, he said.
"Prices of, for example, 450 rand and lower per tonne will push plantings down dramatically and ensure that South Africa in future becomes a net importer of maize," Grobler said.
Official estimates put South Africa's 1996/97 maize crop at 9.48 million tonnes, more than double 1995's drought-reduced 4.41 million.
